blocks.text: 审查瓶颈是一个 ROI 问题

inlines.text: 审查瓶颈是一个 ROI 问题

blocks.text: 评审瓶颈不仅让工程师们倍感压力，也让领导团队倍感压力，因为它是造成 ROI 问题的一大因素。

inlines.text: 评审瓶颈不仅让工程师们倍感压力，也让领导团队倍感压力，因为它是造成 ROI 问题的一大因素。

blocks.text: 所谓“ROI 问题”，我指的是上游代码创建速度的提升远比下游影响更为显著。例如，在 2026 年全年，我们普遍测到拉取请求（PR）数量增长了约 2 倍，但已交付功能等产品产出仅增长了约 40-50%。

inlines.text: 所谓“ROI 问题”，我指的是上游代码创建速度的提升远比下游影响更为显著。例如，在 2026 年全年，我们普遍测到拉取请求（PR）数量增长了约 2 倍，但已交付功能等产品产出仅增长了约 40-50%。

blocks.text: 造成这一差距的原因之一是，由智能体编写的 PR 在早期阶段就失败的比例要高得多。当由人类编写 PR 时，约有 20% 的情况无法合并，原因各种各样且完全正常（例如实验性工作、方案错误、新需求、优先级变化）。而对于智能体，放弃率翻了一倍（40% 对 20%）。与此同时，那些确实合并了的智能体 PR 反而受到更多审查而非更少：过去一年里，每个已合并智能体 PR 所获得的人工评审数量增加了一倍多。

blocks.text: 这些本身都并非不合理。智能体代码确实更难评审，评审者对其保持谨慎是正确的。问题在于，随着编码智能体能力持续增长，这些负担给整个系统带来的压力。评审负担随着智能体产出的增加而扩大，而人类注意力始终是固定的约束，并且我上面展示的自主性曲线每个月都在复利式增长。

inlines.text: 幸运的是，一些公司正在解决这个问题。那些让自主智能体合并 9% PR 的顶尖公司，并不是在盲目地更加信任它们的智能体。相反，它们投入精力来加速信任的建立速度。

blocks.text: 这通常涉及大量平台工作，例如将低风险工作路由给自主智能体的系统、用于安全可靠开发与部署的沙箱和预发布环境，当然还有大量的自动化测试。不过，也许最重要的是，它们很早就开始并大力推进；信任只能随时间建立，你等待得越久，就要越久地忍受不断堆积的评审积压。

blocks.text: Imagine leading an engineering team where you have some major trust issues with 20% of your developers.

blocks.text: These developers are reliable enough that you let them write code, but they require considerable supervision. They can’t be the sole reviewer on other people’s work and they certainly can’t grant approval to merge code to important systems. As developers go, they’re second-class citizens.

blocks.text: Traditional software engineering would view this state of affairs as a serious structural problem. Effective development teams are built on a foundation of trust in high-agency individuals who (along with good processes and safeguards) can write, review, and ship code without needing to be micromanaged.

blocks.text: However, that’s the situation the typical engineering team finds itself in today, except the 20% of developers we’re talking about are AI agents. Most teams require each agent to be chaperoned – and there aren’t enough chaperones to go around.

blocks.text: To anyone who’s been working with AI coding agents in 2026, the incredible adoption of these tools shouldn’t be wildly surprising. Advances in harness and model capability have allowed AI coding agents to take over a large proportion of coding workloads. But that’s just the “raw coding” part, so to speak – you still need to approve, merge, and deploy this code.

blocks.text: So at a typical company, agents are now authoring about a fifth of the code, but almost all of it requires a human at some point in the process. This human oversight is a reasonable way to build trust and ensure quality, but it also represents a hard constraint on how much additional capacity coding agents can provide.

blocks.text: Everyone is talking about software factories, but a factory where every unit has to pass a human inspector before it ships isn’t a factory – it’s just a workshop with more conveyor belts.

blocks.text: The review bottleneck is an ROI problem

inlines.text: The review bottleneck is an ROI problem

blocks.text: The review bottleneck isn’t just stressing out the engineers, it’s also stressing out the leadership team, because it’s a big contributor to the ROI problem.

inlines.text: The review bottleneck isn’t just stressing out the engineers, it’s also stressing out the leadership team, because it’s a big contributor to the ROI problem.

blocks.text: By “ROI problem” I mean that the upstream acceleration of code creation is much more dramatic than the downstream impact. For example, over the course of 2026 we’ve generally measured about a 2x increase in pull requests, but only about a 40-50% increase in product outputs like features shipped.

inlines.text: By “ROI problem” I mean that the upstream acceleration of code creation is much more dramatic than the downstream impact. For example, over the course of 2026 we’ve generally measured about a 2x increase in pull requests, but only about a 40-50% increase in product outputs like features shipped.

blocks.text: One reason for this gap is that agent-authored PRs die on the vine at a much higher rate. When a human authors a PR, it fails to merge about 20% of the time, for all sorts of totally normal reasons (e.g. experimental work, wrong solution, new requirements, changing priorities). For agents though, the abandonment rate is double (40% vs 20%). Meanwhile, the agent PRs that do merge are getting more scrutiny rather than less: over the past year, the number of human reviews per merged agent PR has more than doubled.

blocks.text: None of that is unreasonable on its own. Agent code is genuinely harder to review, and reviewers are right to be careful with it. The problem is the strain these loads put on the system as coding agent capability continues to grow. Review load scales with increasing agent output while human attention remains a fixed constraint, and the autonomy curve I showed above is compounding every month.

blocks.text: If today’s median company gets to where the top 10% are today (with autonomous agents authoring more than half of all code), code review threatens to become the entire job of the human, stealing time from all the other important things that experienced developers need to be doing like collaborating with product and design, shaping software architectures, and bringing their engineering judgment to problems that don’t have clear solutions.

blocks.text: How to build trust faster

inlines.text: How to build trust faster

blocks.text: Fortunately, some companies are figuring this out. The top companies that have autonomous agents merging 9% of PRs aren’t just blindly trusting their agents more. Instead, they’re putting in the work to accelerate how fast trust can be built.

inlines.text: Fortunately, some companies are figuring this out. The top companies that have autonomous agents merging 9% of PRs aren’t just blindly trusting their agents more. Instead, they’re putting in the work to accelerate how fast trust can be built.

blocks.text: Often this entails a lot of platform work, such as systems for routing low-risk work to autonomous agents, sandboxes and staging environments for safe and secure development and deployment, and of course lots and lots of automated testing. Perhaps most importantly though, they’ve started early and are pushing hard; trust can only be built over time, and the longer you wait, the longer you’ll have to live with a mounting review backlog.

inlines.text: Often this entails a lot of platform work, such as systems for routing low-risk work to autonomous agents, sandboxes and staging environments for safe and secure development and deployment, and of course lots and lots of automated testing. Perhaps most importantly though, they’ve started early and are pushing hard; trust can only be built over time, and the longer you wait, the longer you’ll have to live with a mounting review backlog.

blocks.text: Chaperoning every agent is a sensible way to start, but an impossible way to scale.

blocks.text: If you’re interested in learning more about how autonomous agents are evolving (or more accurately, disrupting) the SDLC, come join me at aiDevCon in New York City on November 2–4. I’ll be talking about this and much more in my session Botsitting Doesn’t Scale: How to Navigate the Autonomy-Trust Gridlock in Real Engineering Orgs, and sharing what we’ve learned from analyzing Jellyfish data about how the best engineering teams are tackling the biggest engineering workflow challenges of 2026.
